title: Det. No. 25-0060, 45 WTD 124 (2026)
description: A chiropractic professional services corporation seeks abatement of the assessment penalty and interest on grounds that the corporation’s billing and payment processor suffered a cyberattack preventing the corporation from submitting claims or getting paid, and the corporation was advised to wait for contact from the Department regarding a payment plan. Because the corporation failed to prove that circumstances beyond its control caused the late payment and reliance on oral instructions is not a basis upon which the Department can grant a penalty waiver, we deny the petition.

[1] WAC 458-20-228; RCW 82.32.105; PENALTIES AND INTEREST –
WAIVER – CIRCUMSTANCES BEYOND THE CONTROL OF THE
TAXPAYER – FINANCIAL HARDSHIP. Taxpayer’s payment processor
suffering a cyberattack and failing to timely process claims is not grounds for
waiving penalties and interest.
[2] WAC 458-20-228; RCW 82.32.105; ETA 3065.2009; PENALTIES AND
INTEREST – WAIVER – ORAL INSTRUCTIONS. The law does not permit the
Department to waive penalties or interest based on Taxpayer’s recollection of oral
instructions.
Headnotes are provided as a convenience for the reader and are not in any way a part of the decision
or in any way to be used in construing or interpreting this Determination.
Margolis, T.R.O. – A chiropractic professional services corporation seeks abatement of the
assessment penalty and interest on grounds that the corporation’s billing and payment processor
suffered a cyberattack preventing the corporation from submitting claims or getting paid, and the
corporation was advised to wait for contact from the Department regarding a payment plan.
Because the corporation failed to prove that circumstances beyond its control caused the late
payment and reliance on oral instructions is not a basis upon which the Department can grant a
penalty waiver, we deny the petition.1
ISSUES
1. Whether, under RCW 82.32.105 and WAC 458-20-228, Taxpayer qualifies for waiver of
the assessment penalty and interest on grounds that its billing and payment processor
suffered a cyberattack, so Taxpayer did not have funds to timely pay its tax liability.
1 Identifying details regarding the taxpayer and the assessment have been redacted pursuant to RCW 82.32.410.
Administrative Review & Hearings Division
P O Box 47460 Olympia, WA 98504-7460
dor.wa.gov Phone (360) 534-1335

Det. No. 25-0060, 45 WTD 124 (June 9, 2026) 125
2. Whether, under RCW 82.32.105, WAC 458-20-228, and ETA 3065.2009, Taxpayer’s
assertion that they were told via telephone they would be contacted with respect to a
payment plan is grounds for waiver of penalties and interest.
FINDINGS OF FACT
. . . (Taxpayer) is a . . . Washington provider of chiropractic services. . . .
On February 21, 2024, . . . (Payment Processor), a billing and payment processor, was the subject
of a cyberattack, which prevented health care providers from submitting claims and receiving
payment. Taxpayer’s Annual 2023 return was due on April 15, 2024.2 On April 30, 2024, Taxpayer
filed the return without payment. The return shows a gross amount of $ . . . under the service and
other activities business and occupation (B&O) tax classification, which at the 1.5% rate, results
in tax due of $ . . . . The return states that Taxpayer would like to be considered for a 24-month
penalty waiver, and includes the following explanation:
I am sorry for the delay. I just had a baby at the beginning of April so this report
completely snuck up on me. We also have been subject to the cyber-attack on
[Payment Processor] (we are a chiropractic clinic) so we haven’t had insurance
payments since Feb 21st. We are really hurting for cash until that starts coming in
again.
On May 13, 2024, the Department issued a Notice of Balance Due against Taxpayer for $ . . . , due
June 12, 2024. This amount is composed of $ . . . in service and other activities B&O tax, a $ . . .
5-percent assessment penalty, a $ . . . 9-percent delinquent penalty, and $ . . . in interest. Taxpayer
failed to pay by June 12, 2024. On June 13, 2024, the Department increased the assessment penalty
to $ . . . (15-percent), and on July 13, 2024, the Department increased the assessment penalty to $
. . . (25-percent). On July 31, 2024, Taxpayer paid $ . . . , and sent a message to the Department
that reads, in pertinent part, as follows:3
I submitted this request before the tax portion of our amount due was paid. I have
now paid the tax portion and would love if you could reconsider waiving the
penalties and interest. We are not the kind of people who are intentionally late on
things or don’t pay something but we had an unexpected circumstance happen in
February of this year that completely decimated our cash flow. On Feb 21st 2024 a
cyber attack happened to [Payment Processor] which is our clearing house that we
use to submit insurance claims. We were unable to submit insurance claims OR get
paid for claims already submitted until the end of May 2024. This was a very scary
time for our business and the reason that we were unable to pay our B&O tax.
2 https://dor.wa.gov/file-pay-taxes/filing-frequencies-due-dates/filing-due-dates/2023-excise-tax-return-due-dates
(last accessed March 3, 2025).
3 RCW 82.32.080(5)(a) provides that the Department must apply payments to interest and penalties first, without
regard to any direction of the taxpayer. Thus, tax liability remained after the payment, and interest continued to accrue
on that remaining tax liability.

On September 5, 2024, the Department’s Taxpayer Account Administration Division (TAA)
responded to the message, explaining that the request for a 24-month waiver was approved (noting
that it does not apply to the assessment penalty), and waived the $ . . . 9-percent delinquent penalty.
On September 10, 2024, Taxpayer petitioned for correction of the assessment penalty and interest.
Taxpayer does not contest that the subject penalties and interest were properly imposed; it merely
seeks a waiver of the penalties and interest. Taxpayer asserts that the Payment Processor
cyberattack resulted in Taxpayer being unable to submit insurance claims or get paid for claims
already submitted until the end of May 2024, which impacted its cash flow and its ability to pay
anything other than rent and payroll and prevented Taxpayer from timely paying the Department.
Taxpayer also asserts that it called the Department on April 30, 2024 – approximately two weeks
after the subject return was due – to discuss the overdue balance. Taxpayer asserts that the
Department representative they spoke to told Taxpayer to file the return with no payment and
someone would contact Taxpayer to set up a payment plan, but nobody contacted Taxpayer. As a
result, additional liability accrued. While Department records confirm a telephone call took place
on April 30, 2024, no notes or other records with respect to the call indicate that a Department
agent advised Taxpayer to wait for contact regarding a payment plan for the 2023 period.
ANALYSIS
RCW 82.32A.030 provides that taxpayers have the responsibility to pay taxes in a timely manner.
If the Department obtains information from which it appears a person has not paid the amount of
tax properly due, then the Department is required to assess any additional amounts found due
against that person and is also required to add interest to the tax due. RCW 82.32.050.
RCW 82.32.090(2) states that there is assessed a penalty of 5-percent when the Department
determines that a taxpayer has substantially underpaid a tax that was due. If payment is not
received by the due date specified in the notice, there is assessed a total penalty of 15-percent and,
if payment is not received on or before the thirtieth day following the due date specified in the
notice, there is assessed a total penalty of 25-percent. “Substantially underpaid” means the
taxpayer has paid less than 80 percent of the tax due and the underpayment is at least $1,000.00. Id.
1. Waiver on Grounds of Cyberattack
The Department has limited authority to waive or cancel penalties under RCW 82.32.105.
Generally, the Department will not waive penalties unless the failure that triggered the penalty was
the result of “circumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer.” RCW 82.32.105(1).
WAC 458-20-228 (Rule 228) explains that “[c]ircumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer
are generally those which are immediate, unexpected, or in the nature of an emergency. Such
circumstances result in the taxpayer not having reasonable time or opportunity to obtain an
extension of the due date or otherwise timely file and pay.” Rule 228(9)(a)(ii). The burden is on
the taxpayer to establish that “the circumstances were beyond its control and directly caused the
late payment.” Rule 228(9)(a)(i).
Administrative Review & Hearings Division
P O Box 47460 Olympia, WA 98504-7460
dor.wa.gov Phone (360) 534-1335

Det. No. 25-0060, 45 WTD 124 (June 9, 2026) 127
In this matter, Taxpayer argues that a cyberattack suffered by Payment Processor resulted in
Taxpayer not having sufficient cash to timely pay its tax liability. Examples of what generally
constitutes circumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer are provided in Rule 228(9)(a)(ii),
none of which apply to the situation under consideration.4 Rule 228(9)(a)(iii) also gives examples
of circumstances that are generally not considered to be a basis for waiving penalties.5 This
includes financial hardship.
In Det. No. 87-189, 3 WTD 223 (1987), the taxpayer was in the healthcare business, received
approximately 40 percent of its income from the state of Washington, and the state’s payments
were frequently months delinquent. We concluded that the state’s late payment of amounts due to
the taxpayer could not justify a penalty waiver, explaining as follows:
It makes no difference that the state is the contracting party with the taxpayer. Our
holding would be the same even if the contracting party were a private business. In
other words, a person’s tax liability is an absolute; it is no defense that other third
4 Examples of circumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer in Rule 228(9)(a)(ii) include:
(A) The return payment was mailed on time but inadvertently sent to another agency.
(B) Erroneous written information given to the taxpayer by a department officer or employee caused the delinquency
. . . .
(C) The delinquency was directly caused by death or serious illness of the taxpayer, or a member of the taxpayer’s
immediate family . . . .
(D) The delinquency was caused by the unavoidable absence of the taxpayer or key employee, prior to the filing date.
“Unavoidable absence of the taxpayer” does not include absences because of business trips, vacations, personnel
turnover, or terminations.
(E) The delinquency was caused by the destruction by fire or other casualty of the taxpayer’s place of business or
business records.
(F) The delinquency was caused by an act of fraud, embezzlement, theft, or conversion on the part of the taxpayer’s
employee or other persons contracted with the taxpayer, which the taxpayer could not immediately detect or prevent,
provided that reasonable safeguards or internal controls were in place. See (a)(iii)(E) of this subsection.
(G) The department does not respond to the taxpayer’s request for a tax return (or other forms necessary to compute
the tax) within a reasonable period of time, which directly causes delinquent filing and payment on the part of the
taxpayer. This assumes that, given the same situation, if the department had provided the requested form(s) within a
reasonable period of time, the taxpayer would have been able to meet its obligation for timely payment of the tax. In
any case, the taxpayer has responsibility to insure that its return is filed in a timely manner (e.g., by keeping track of
pending due dates) and must anticipatively request a return for that purpose, if one is not received . . . .
5 Examples in Rule 228(9)(a)(iii) of circumstances that are generally not beyond the control of the taxpayer and will
not qualify for waiver or cancellation of penalty include:
(A) Financial hardship;
(B) A misunderstanding or lack of knowledge of a tax liability;
(C) The failure of the taxpayer to receive a tax return form, EXCEPT where the taxpayer timely requested the form
and it was still not furnished in reasonable time to mail the return and payment by the due date, as described in
(a)(ii)(G) of this subsection;
(D) Registration of an account that is not considered a voluntary registration, as described in subsection (5)(a)(iii) and
(b) of this section;
(E) Mistakes or misconduct on the part of employees or other persons contracted with the taxpayer (not including
conduct covered in (a)(ii)(F) of this subsection); and
(F) Reliance upon unpublished, written information from the department that was issued to and specifically addresses
the circumstances of some other taxpayer.

parties owe the taxpayer money with which the taxes could have more easily been
made.
Here, Taxpayer alleges that cash flow problems prevented timely payment. However, financial
hardship is not grounds for waiver, regardless of whether Payment Processor suffered a
cyberattack and failed to timely process claims. Thus, we find that the cyberattack was not a
circumstance beyond Taxpayer’s control that qualifies Taxpayer for waiver. See also, Det. No. 06-
0267, 26 WTD 159 (2007). Further, we note that Taxpayer’s waiver request submitted with its
return explains that the late filing was also due to an error on account of a newborn, but mistakes
are generally not considered beyond the control of the taxpayer per Rule 228(9)(a)(iii)(E). Because
Taxpayer failed to prove that “circumstances beyond the control of the taxpayer” directly caused
the late payment, we conclude that Taxpayer does not qualify for waiver of the assessment penalty.
RCW 82.32.105(3) and Rule 228(10) provide that the Department will waive or
cancel interest imposed under chapter 82.32 RCW only where the failure to pay the tax prior to
the issuance of the assessment was the direct result of written instructions given the taxpayer by
the Department, or the extension of the due date for payment of an assessment was not at the
request of the taxpayer and was for the sole convenience of the Department. Since we find no
evidence of either of these circumstances in the petition or record, these provisions provide no
grounds for abatement of interest.
2. Waiver on Grounds of Oral Advice
Taxpayer argues that it was given oral advice to wait for contact regarding a payment plan, which
resulted in the accrual of additional liability. Rule 228(9)(a)(ii)(B) provides, in pertinent part, that
[a] penalty generally will not be waived when it is claimed that erroneous oral
information was given by a department employee. The reason for not canceling the
penalty in cases of oral information is because of the uncertainty of the facts
presented, the uncertainty of the instructions or information imparted by the
department employee, and the uncertainty that the taxpayer fully understood the
information given. . . [.]
Excise Tax Advisory (ETA) 3065.20096 discusses oral instructions related to tax liability as
follows:
RCW 82.32A.020 provides that the taxpayers of Washington have:: [sic]
The right to rely on specific, official written advice and written tax
reporting instructions from the department of revenue to that
taxpayer, and to have interest, penalties, and in some instances, tax
deficiency assessments waived where the taxpayer has so relied to
their proven detriment.
6 ETAs are interpretive statements authorized by RCW 34.05.230.
Administrative Review & Hearings Division
P O Box 47460 Olympia, WA 98504-7460
dor.wa.gov Phone (360) 534-1335

Det. No. 25-0060, 45 WTD 124 (June 9, 2026) 129
RCW 82.32A.020 does not authorize, nor does any other law permit, the
Department to waive tax, interest, or penalties on the basis of a taxpayer’s
recollection of oral instructions by an agent of the department.
The Department gives consideration, to the extent of discretion vested in it by law,
where it can be shown that failure of a taxpayer to report correctly was due to
written instructions from the Department or any of its authorized agents. The
Department cannot give consideration to claimed misinformation resulting from
telephone conversations or personal consultations with a Department employee.
There are three reasons for this ruling:
(1) There is no record of the facts which might have been presented
to the employee for consideration.
(2) There is no record of instructions or information imparted by the
employee, which may have been erroneous or incomplete.
(3) There is no evidence that such instructions were completely
understood or followed by the taxpayer.
(Underlining in original.)
Because we find no written evidence that Taxpayer was advised to pay nothing and wait for contact
regarding a payment plan, and the law does not permit the Department to waive penalties or interest
based on Taxpayer’s recollection of oral instructions, we find no grounds for relief.
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer’s petition is denied.
Dated this 10th day of March 2025.
